title: The Debate That’s Missing from “Sold A Story”
author: Daniel Willingham
summary: Daniel Willingham argues that Season 2 of Sold a Story frames Direct Instruction as a case of evidence ignored, when the real disagreement is partly about what schooling is for. He lists why DI works in cognitive terms: knowledge-rich content, careful sequencing, high student response, feedback to the teacher and tightly controlled attention. He grants the evidence for strong academic outcomes, especially in foundational skills, though it is sometimes overstated. But the same features offend those who want children to have intellectual agency, follow spontaneous interests and combine learning with social development and creativity. He says that is a value judgment, not an empirical claim, and asks both sides to name the tradeoffs: critics must say how much achievement they would sacrifice, and DI advocates must accept that evidence alone does not settle the matter.
points: Season 1 of Sold a Story was about the best method for a shared goal; Season 2 touches on what the goal of schooling should be.
DI aligns with cognitive principles through knowledge richness, sequencing, student response, teacher feedback and controlled attention.
The features that produce DI's results are the ones objectors dislike: teacher control of speech and attention, adult-structured lessons, and academics separated from social and creative development.
Preferring children's autonomy as part of childhood is a value judgment, not an empirical prediction, and should be owned as such.
Critics must say what they propose and how much achievement they would trade away, and DI advocates should not think evidence alone settles the debate.

But the features that support those good results are, I believe, exactly the ones that some adults find objectionable.
But one might also believe that children should have opportunities to exercise autonomy simply because it’s an important part of childhood. That’s a value judgment, not an empirical prediction.
At the same time, claiming “this conflicts with my values” is not a pass to ignore evidence. If you spurn a pedagogy because of what students will experience, you need to own it.
And if you’re a DI advocate, you’re right to emphasize the evidence for academic achievement. But you’re wrong if you think that alone settles the debate.
